::: {.lede}
I study where authority and public money actually sit inside developing
countries, and what that placement does to the places people live.
:::

I am a Research Officer in Economic Geography and Spatial Economics at LSE's
Department of Geography and Environment and Global School of Sustainability,
and Lecturer in Urban Economics at the African School of Economics' Africa
Urban Lab. I am also a DPhil candidate in Sustainable Urban Development at the
University of Oxford, where I am a Doctoral Affiliate of the Centre for the
Study of African Economies and a Research Affiliate of the Blavatnik School of
Government.

[**Fields:** urban and regional economics; political economy of development;
economic geography. **Regions:** sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.]{.fields}

::: {.featured}
[Featured paper]{.label}

[Status without Power: The Political Economy of Administrative Unit Creation in Uganda]{.paper-title}

Uganda has repeatedly carved new administrative units out of old ones, often
for political reasons. This paper treats that politically selected, block
adoption of new units as a quasi-experiment and uses a staggered
difference-in-differences design with spatial structure to measure what the
new units actually do once they exist.

[More on my research](research.qmd#featured-paper) &nbsp; Draft available on request
:::

My research has two strands. The first, and the subject of my thesis,
*Power and Place*, is decentralisation and the provision of local public goods
in African cities. I built a framework of capacity, authority and means,
applied it to eight countries over three decades, and extended the Hooghe–Marks
Regional Authority Index to the metropolitan tier, coding national legislation
with large language models and validating the codings with in-country experts.
The second strand asks how foreign investment and global value chains land in
particular regions, and whether those regions capture anything durable from
them as the economy turns green.

Before and alongside the doctorate, I spent a decade working with city
governments and national ministries across Africa, Asia and the Caribbean: as
Cities Economist and then Senior Policy Economist on the International Growth
Centre's [Cities that Work](https://www.theigc.org/initiatives/cities-work)
initiative, and as an ODI Fellow in Guyana's Ministry of Communities. That
[policy work](policy.qmd) has been taken up by decision-makers in 27 countries.

I [teach](teaching.qmd) urban economics at LSE and the Africa Urban Lab, and
co-convened the BREAD-IGC virtual PhD course in urban economics with Edward
Glaeser. In 2026 I received the Class Teacher Award in LSE's Department of
Geography and Environment.

This site collects my [research](research.qmd), [teaching](teaching.qmd),
[policy work](policy.qmd) and [commentary](commentary.qmd).

My best email is <o.harman@lse.ac.uk>, and I am on
[Google Scholar](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=SLb3QHIAAAAJ) and
[LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/oharman/). If you are ever in London or
Oxford, I am nearly always available for a cup of tea.
